title: A Million Words or Fewer, Deborah Bova's Method for Learning from Parents at the Start of Distance Learning
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. introduces Deborah Bova's "Million Words or Less" activity — inviting parents to write, in as many or as few words as they choose, about their child at the start of the year — as his preferred method for gathering sensitive family context during distance learning. He traces the activity's origin to a 2003 teacher listserv post and explains why it works: it's simple and non-intimidating for parents, it visibly demonstrates a school-home partnership rather than just claiming one, and it keeps the teacher humble by centering the family's voice rather than the teacher's assumptions. Stuart argues the activity is especially valuable during distance learning because it surfaces information — trauma, tech access issues, family stress — that a "warmly demanding" teacher needs in order to serve students equitably. He shares that he's using a simplified version of the introductory letter with his own students' families this year and credits several colleagues for helping refine the practice.
points: The Million Words activity works because it's low-friction for parents — they set their own word count, which removes the intimidation of a formal survey.
Stuart frames the activity as demonstrating (not just claiming) a school-home partnership, since it visibly asks parents for their expertise on their own child.
He connects the practice to "warm demander" pedagogy: the family context gathered is what allows a teacher to hold high expectations equitably rather than blindly.
The activity doubles as a humility exercise for the teacher, reframing them as a "side character" in students' lives rather than the protagonist.
quotes: One thing that I would suggest to new and returnee teachers is something I call 'In a million words or less, tell us about your child,' Bova wrote.
It's invitational. Parents are being invited to play a key role in introducing their child to their teacher or teaching team. They are free to write as little or as much as they can.
It's far more humanizing than a survey. The "data" something like this elicits will humanize students for us like no survey ever can.

When I get a stack of Million Words responses back and I sit down to them with a cup of coffee, I'm training my heart to marvel at the weight of my students and the trust implied in their coming to be with me each day.
If my students have specific life circumstances that will prove an obstacle to distance learning, I need to know. If they've experienced trauma during the pandemic, I need to know.
Such information readies me to be the kind of warmly demanding (v. perversely compassionate) teacher that equitable school outcomes require.
